title: Hearsay: 〜そうだ, 〜って, 〜らしい

grammarPoints.rule: そうだ reports what you HEARD, not what you see. Take a complete plain-form sentence — dictionary-form verb, plain い-adjective, or noun/な-adjective plus だ — and add そうだ at the end: あめが ふるそうだ, 'I heard it's going to rain.' The whole clause in front of そうだ stays exactly as you would say it on its own; nothing is trimmed. That full-form attachment is the one thing that tells this apart from module 36's appearance そう (ふりそう, stem only, い/だ dropped) — a different word doing a different job, met properly much later in the course. For a noun or な-adjective, だ is required before そうだ: びょうきだそうだ (I heard he's sick), not びょうきそうだ. Politely, the ending becomes そうです — ふるそうです — and you will hear Tanaka use it; you build with the plain form.

examples.en: I heard the reporter is sick.

examples.en: I heard it's going to rain.

examples.en: I heard the show is interesting.

examples.en: I heard there was an earthquake.

antiPattern.why: そうだ hangs on a COMPLETE clause, and a noun needs its copula だ first: びょうきだそうだ, 'I heard he's sick.' Dropping だ gives m36's appearance そう instead — 'looks sick' — a different word for a different job, met at hearsay そうだ's spot only through its full-form だ.

grammarPoints.rule: って is casual spoken quoting — the everyday shortcut for と言っていた. Put a complete plain-form sentence in front of it and って hands it over exactly the way と does: たなかさんが くるって, 'Tanaka said he's coming' (compare the more formal たなかさんが くると いっていた, same meaning, module 18's と plus this module's いっていた). Reach for って with friends, drop it for teachers or strangers — that register gap is the whole reason it exists next to と. It attaches after ANY plain sentence, questions included: なんで こないって？'why did they say they're not coming?'

examples.en: Tanaka said he's coming.

antiPattern.ja: たなかさんが くるとって。
antiPattern.why: って already does と's job by itself — it does not stack on top of と. Drop the と: たなかさんが くるって, 'Tanaka said he's coming.'

grammarPoints.rule: と言っていた reports what someone said, in the past, with the register-neutral と you already own from module 18 (と言う, と思う). と closes the exact plain sentence they said — 「あした いく」と いっていた, 'she said she was going tomorrow' — and いっていた (was saying, said) carries the report itself in the past. It is the formal partner to this module's own って: 「あした いく」と いっていた and あした いくって say the same thing, one careful, one casual. Politely, いっていました — Tanaka's register, not yours to build with yet.

examples.ja: たなかさんは たいふうが くると いっていた。

antiPattern.ja: ミカは あした くるが いっていた。
antiPattern.why: が marks a subject, and a whole quoted sentence is not a subject — it is handed over with と, exactly as module 18 taught: ミカは あした くると いっていた。

grammarPoints.rule: らしい is hearsay one step further back than そうだ — it says 'apparently,' from indirect evidence, not a direct report you can point to. It attaches to a complete plain-form clause the same way そうだ does: あの みせは おいしいらしい, 'apparently that shop is good.' For a noun or な-adjective, unlike そうだ, らしい does NOT need だ first: びょうきらしい (apparently he's sick), never びょうきだらしい. It behaves like any い-adjective after that point — らしかった for the past. Reach for らしい when you are passing along an impression, not quoting a specific source: そうだ says 'I heard X'; らしい says 'it seems X, from what's around.'

antiPattern.why: らしい attaches directly after a noun or な-adjective with no だ — だ belongs to そうだ's pattern, not らしい's: きしゃは びょうきらしい, 'apparently the reporter is sick.'

turns.replyGloss: I heard it's coming, but according to the rumor, they say it's not coming.
turns.explanation: そうだ carries the direct 'I heard' report; けど sets up the contrast; って closes the rumor's own quoted claim. らしい would soften the claim instead of reporting it directly — the wrong tool for 'I heard.'

beats.ja: あめが ふるそうだ。
beats.en: I heard it's going to rain.

beats.ja: たいふうが くるって。
beats.en: They said a typhoon is coming.

beats.ja: きしゃは じこが あったと いっていた。
beats.en: The reporter said there was an accident.

beats.stem: きしゃは びょうき
beats.en: Apparently the reporter is sick.
beats.explanation: らしい attaches straight after a noun with no だ. だらしい does not exist, and そうだ would need だ first — a different word with a different rule.

beats.ja: ほうそうで じしんの はっぴょうが あった。

lessons.title: Challenge — three ways to say you heard
lessons.focus: Every hearsay marker in one arc — そうだ, って, と言っていた, らしい — combined with prior N4 grammar, no new vocabulary

beats.ja: ニュースで じしんが あったと いっていたので、きじを よんだら、たいふうも くるそうだった。
beats.en: Since the news said there was an earthquake, when I read the article, I heard a typhoon was coming too.

beats.ja: うわさで は じこが あったって いっているし、きしゃも それを つたえたらしいから、じこは あっただろう。
beats.en: The rumor says there was an accident, and what's more apparently the reporter conveyed that too, so there was probably an accident.

beats.tail: し、あめも ふるらしいのに、はっぴょうは まだ ない。
beats.en: I heard a typhoon is coming, and what's more apparently it will rain too, even though there's no announcement yet.
beats.explanation: The clause after のに already reports rain with らしい, so the first clause keeps its own distinct marker — そうだ, a direct hearsay report, not a repeat of らしい.

lines.speaker: Tanaka
lines.ja: たいふうは くるんですか。
lines.en: So, is the typhoon coming?

lines.speaker: Mika
lines.ja: きしゃは くると いっていたが、うわさで は こないって いっている人も います。
lines.en: The reporter said it was coming, but according to rumor there are also people saying it's not.

lines.speaker: Ken
lines.ja: ほうそうの はっぴょうを まったほうが いいらしいですね。
lines.en: Apparently it's better to wait for the broadcast's announcement.

questions.q: What do people disagree about, per the conversation?

beats.ja: きしゃは じこが あったと いっていたし、うわさでも たいふうが くるって きいたから、はっぴょうが あるまで、うちに いったほうが いいらしい。
beats.en: The reporter said there was an accident, and what's more I heard a rumor that a typhoon is coming too, so apparently it's better to go home until there's an announcement.
